Take a photograph and make a photocopy. Then a photocopy of the
photocopy. Do it again. And again.

If you keep going long enough, the picture is gone. What's on the page
is grey noise that could plausibly have started as almost anything. The
information about the original has been erased.

This is a familiar form of loss. Each pass through the copier loses a
little, the losses pile up, and eventually nothing remains. Heat works
this way too. So does mixing dye into water, or scrambling a Rubik's
cube, or letting milk cool in a glass. Everywhere you look, processes
that destroy information are processes that destroy it in *steps*:
many small irreversible nudges that add up.

Now think about how you'd design such a process. You have full control
of the photocopier. The cheap thing you can do is make it violently
destructive: a single pass turns any input into grey noise. Erasure in
one step. Done.

You can also build copiers that never quite finish in any finite number
of passes, and only erase everything in the infinite limit of repeated
copying. This is a genuinely interesting region of design space.
Characterising which copiers really do erase everything in the limit
(as opposed to settling onto some non-trivial steady image, or
oscillating, or simply slowing to a crawl) is the subject of a
substantial literature on ergodic and mixing channels.[^mixing-ref] It
is not, however, the question of this post.

This post's question sits between those two. How *slowly* can you
erase, while still finishing in finitely many steps?

Concretely: among all copy-of-a-copy operations that erase the
original after some exact number $k$ of identical applications, how
large can $k$ be?

[^mixing-ref]: TODO: pick one of the candidate references suggested in
chat (e.g. Burgarth et al. 2013 on ergodic/mixing channels, or Sanz et
al. 2010 on the quantum Wielandt inequality), or Michael Wolf's
*Quantum Channels & Operations: Guided Tour* lecture notes for a more
pedagogical entry point.

There's a second way to picture the same question, and it's the one
that makes the problem feel physical. A quantum device you use over and
over (a logic gate, a link down a fibre) need not treat each use
independently: it can carry a private *memory* from one use to the next,
a lingering excitation or stray correlation that makes what it does now
lean on its history. Such a device is *forgetful* when the influence of
how that memory started eventually washes out (the asymptotic case from
a moment ago), and *strictly forgetful* when the washout is *exact*,
every trace of the initial memory provably gone after some finite number
of uses. Not small, gone.

And with no separate input to track, a device that becomes strictly
forgetful after exactly $k$ uses is nothing but a $k$-th root of
complete erasure.[^memory-channels] To ask how finely we can divide
erasure is to ask how long a finite quantum memory can survive before it
is forced to forget exactly, and the largest $k$ is the deepest such
memory a device of this kind can hold.

[^memory-channels]: The framework of quantum channels with memory is due
to D. Kretschmann and R. F. Werner, "Quantum channels with memory,"
*Phys. Rev. A* **72**, 062323 (2005); arXiv:quant-ph/0502106.

That largest $k$ is where this post lives, and it has different answers
in different settings. If the copier has to behave like a classical
probabilistic process, you get one bound. Upgrade to quantum mechanics,
and the bound becomes *quadratically* larger. Then restrict the quantum
copier to a tightly constrained, low-parameter family of operations, a
family with vastly less freedom than the general quantum case, and you
might expect the bound to drop most of the way back down.

It almost doesn't. The factor-of-2 gap that remains is the punchline.
The reason it remains is a piece of finite-field bookkeeping that
turns out, if you sit with it, to be unreasonably beautiful.

<!-- =================================================================== -->
## The classical setup {#sec-classical}

Let's make the photocopier mathematically precise. We start with the
classical case, where everything is ordinary probability theory.

Pick a small number of distinct states your image can be in. Say
three, and to keep them vivid, call them red, green, and blue. At any
moment a pixel of the image need not be one definite colour. Noise has
crept in, and the honest description is a list of how likely each
colour is. Right now it might be definitely red. After a few passes
through the copier, it might be 40% red, 50% green, 10% blue.

We write that list as a vector. Definitely red is $(1, 0, 0)$; the
blurred state is $(0.4, 0.5, 0.1)$, read in the order red, green, blue.
Two rules turn a list of numbers into a probability distribution, and
we lean on both later. The entries cannot be negative, since a
probability below zero is meaningless. And they must sum to one, since
the pixel is certainly *some* colour. Every classical state we write
obeys these two rules, and nothing else counts.

Now picture all the lawful states at once. With three colours a state
is three numbers summing to one, so fixing any two pins the third: only
two are free. Two free numbers trace out a flat, two-dimensional shape,
and that shape is a triangle. Its three corners are the sure things,
one per colour: $(1,0,0)$ is definitely red, $(0,1,0)$ definitely
green, $(0,0,1)$ definitely blue. Walk along an edge joining two
corners and the third colour stays impossible while the other two trade
off. Drift inward and all three grow likelier together, until at the
dead centre you reach $(\tfrac13, \tfrac13, \tfrac13)$: an even wash of
red, green, and blue with no colour favoured, the state that could have
come from anything. That even wash is exactly the grey noise from the
start of this post, the worn-out photocopy written as a vector, and
pushing every corner toward it is the whole job of an erasing copier.
The triangle has a name, the *simplex*, and for $d$ states it becomes
the $(d-1)$-dimensional version of the same idea (@fig-simplex-d3).

::: {#fig-simplex-d3}

{{< include figures/fig1-state-space/interactive.qmd >}}

The classical state space for three outcomes: the probability simplex
sitting inside the positive octant. Its three pure states sit at the
vertices, marked in red, green, and blue, and the uniform distribution
$p_0 = (\tfrac13, \tfrac13, \tfrac13)$ is the grey point at the centre,
an even wash of all three. The fill separately encodes purity, saturated
at the pure corners and fading toward the maximally mixed centre.

:::

A copy operation takes one probability distribution as input and
returns another. Before we write down what kind of object such an
operation is, it is worth asking what we want to insist on.

The first thing is *linearity*. The copier $S$ has to be a linear
map: if you feed it a coin-flip mixture of two inputs, the output has
to be the same coin-flip mixture of the two separate outputs. Anything
else would let the copier react to information beyond what the input
distribution actually contains, which is a contradiction in terms.

```{=html}
<details class="aside">
<summary>Why must mixtures behave this way?</summary>
```

Suppose you decide your input on the flip of a coin: with probability
$\alpha$ you start from distribution $p$, and with probability
$1 - \alpha$ you start from $q$. The total input, before you flip the
coin, is the mixture $\alpha p + (1 - \alpha) q$.

Apply the copier $S$. You can describe what comes out in two ways. From
inside the experiment, the output is "$S(p)$ with probability $\alpha$,
$S(q)$ otherwise," which is the distribution
$\alpha S(p) + (1 - \alpha) S(q)$. From outside, ignoring the coin flip,
you simply fed the copier a single mixture, so the output is
$S(\alpha p + (1 - \alpha) q)$.

These two descriptions had better agree:
$$
S\bigl(\alpha p + (1 - \alpha) q\bigr) \;=\; \alpha S(p) + (1 - \alpha) S(q).
$$
If they disagreed, "the input is a probability distribution" would stop
meaning what we want it to mean. So $S$ is linear.

```{=html}
</details>
```

A linear map of vectors is exactly a matrix, so from here on our copier
is a matrix, which we will call $S$, and applying it to a distribution
is ordinary matrix-times-vector multiplication.

It is worth seeing what that does to our three corners, because it pins
down the whole matrix. Feed in pure red, the vector $(1, 0, 0)$.
Multiplying $S$ by a vector that is all zeros except for a single one
just reads off the matching column, so the output is the first column of
$S$: whatever $S$ does to red lives there. Pure green $(0, 1, 0)$ picks
out the second column, pure blue $(0, 0, 1)$ the third. The three
columns of $S$ are therefore nothing but the images of the three pure
states, the three places the corners are sent, and once those are fixed
linearity supplies every blend in between.

That already constrains the entries. Each column is the image of a pure
state, and that image has to be a legal state in its own right: its
entries non-negative and summing to one,
$$
S_{ij} \geq 0, \qquad \sum_i S_{ij} = 1.
$$
The same holds for every column, and linearity then takes care of every
mixture in between. A matrix of this kind, non-negative entries with
every column summing to one, is called a *stochastic matrix*: exactly
the linear maps that send probability distributions to probability
distributions.

There is one more restriction we will impose, and it turns out to
be the most interesting one in retrospect. We will only consider
copiers that leave the *uniform distribution* untouched, the grey
centre of the triangle from a moment ago: the flat distribution that
puts equal weight on every state has to come back out exactly as it
went in.

Why? The uniform distribution represents *no information* about the
state of the image: every outcome equally likely. It is also the
destination. The grey centre is exactly where an erasing copier is
trying to send everything, so a process whose job is to forget should
come to rest there once it arrives, not stir the grey back into a
sharper image. A copier that instead turned "no information" into "some
information" would be generating knowledge out of nothing, and leaving
the grey centre fixed is the natural way to forbid that. (In the
quantum upgrade later in the post, the analogous restriction is more
than just natural, it is the standard convention. For now, take it as a
sensible thing to ask for.)

This small demand has a tidy consequence. We already know the columns
of $S$ sum to one. Insisting that the uniform distribution survives
forces the *rows* to sum to one as well. A stochastic matrix with that
extra symmetry is called *bistochastic*, and from here on "copier" will
mean "bistochastic matrix."

```{=html}
<details class="aside">
<summary>The one-line computation</summary>
```

Write $u = (1/d, \ldots, 1/d)$ for the uniform distribution and ask for
$Su = u$. Reading off entry $i$ of the output,
$$
(Su)_i \;=\; \sum_j S_{ij} \cdot \frac{1}{d}
\;=\; \frac{1}{d} \sum_j S_{ij}
\;\overset{!}{=}\; \frac{1}{d},
$$
which is exactly $\sum_j S_{ij} = 1$ for every row $i$.

```{=html}
</details>
```

One small fact worth pinning down before we go further: the product
of two bistochastic matrices is bistochastic, which you can verify
directly from the row and column sum conditions. So $S^k$ stays
bistochastic for any $k$, and the question of finite roots is going
to be a question about powers of matrices that stay safely inside
our chosen class.

Now we can say precisely what "total erasure" means. The most
depolarising copier you can write down is the one whose every column
is the uniform distribution. Every input state, no matter which one,
produces the same uniform output:
$$
P = \frac{1}{d}\begin{pmatrix}
1 & 1 & \cdots & 1 \\
1 & 1 & \cdots & 1 \\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
1 & 1 & \cdots & 1
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Apply $P$ to anything and you get the uniform distribution back. All
information about the input has been thrown away in a single step.
Apply $P$ again and nothing changes: the simplex has contracted to
a single point, the centre, and $P$ just keeps mapping it there.
This $P$ is bistochastic by inspection (every row sums to one as
well), and it is the *completely depolarising channel* in dimension
$d$, or CDC for short.

With $P$ pinned down, the question we opened with stops being a story
about photocopiers and becomes one line of mathematics. The copier that
erases in steps, the demand that it finish after exactly $k$ identical
passes: all of it is now this. Here $k$ is a positive integer, the number of passes. A *$k$-th root* of
$P$ is a bistochastic matrix $S$ for which
$$
\boxed{\; S^k = P, \qquad S^j \neq P \ \text{ for every integer } 1 \le j < k. \;}
$$
Spelled out: apply the copier $S$ exactly $k$ times and you get $P$,
total erasure; apply it any smaller whole number of times, one pass, two,
up to $k-1$, and the erasure has not happened yet. Both $k$ and $j$ count
applications, so they are positive integers, and the second condition
runs over every one of them below $k$. The first equation is the whole
post in miniature, a single copier that erases totally in $k$ identical
steps; the second pins $k$ down as the *exact* number, the erasure
landing at step $k$ and not one sooner. Everything from here on is the
hunt for such an $S$ with $k$ as large as possible, and the difficulty
(and the beauty) is finding a *non-trivial* one, an $S$ that is not
simply $P$ itself. How large can $k$ be?

The smallest case settles itself. A two-state bistochastic matrix has a
single free number,
$$
S = \begin{pmatrix} 1-a & a \\ a & 1-a \end{pmatrix},
$$
and $P$ is the case $a = \tfrac12$. Its one direction away from the grey
centre, $v = (1,-1)$, is merely rescaled,
$$
Sv = (1-2a)\,v,
$$
so $S^k$ scales it by $(1-2a)^k$. Asking $S^k = P$ forces $(1-2a)^k = 0$,
and a number powers to zero only if it was already zero. So $a = \tfrac12$
and $S = P$ from the start: one classical bit has no genuine root,
$k = 1$, erasure in a single shot.

Three states are the first with room to spare, and the clean way to find
that room is to stop guessing whole matrices and split off the part that
does the forgetting. Every copier in our class fixes the grey centre, so
write
$$
S = P + N,
$$
with $P$ the completely depolarising channel and $N$ whatever is left
over. Two facts about $P$ make this split pay off. It is idempotent,
$P^2 = P$, and it absorbs $N$ from both sides, $PN = NP = 0$ (the columns
of $N$ sum to zero because those of $S$ and $P$ both sum to one, and its
rows sum to zero because $S$ fixes the uniform state). Square $S$ and the
cross terms vanish:
$$
S^2 = (P + N)^2 = P^2 + PN + NP + N^2 = P + N^2.
$$
The question has collapsed. $S^2 = P$ holds exactly when $N^2 = 0$. We no
longer need a square root of $P$; we need a single nonzero $N$ that
squares to zero and keeps $P + N$ a legal copier.

So solve $N^2 = 0$ directly. The condition is stricter than it looks. If
$N$ squares to zero it can have rank at most one, which means it is a
single outer product,
$$
N = u\,v^{\mathsf T},
$$
and then all three demands become conditions on the two vectors alone:
$$
N^2 = 0 \iff v^{\mathsf T} u = 0, \qquad
\textstyle\sum_i u_i = 0, \qquad
\textstyle\sum_j v_j = 0,
$$
the last two being the vanishing column and row sums. In words: take any
two vectors that are orthogonal and that each sum to zero. That is the
whole recipe.

```{=html}
<details class="aside">
<summary>Why $N^2 = 0$ forces rank one</summary>
```

If $N^2 = 0$ then $N$ sends everything into its own kernel: for any $x$,
$N(Nx) = 0$, so $\operatorname{im} N \subseteq \ker N$. Their dimensions
add to the full size, $\operatorname{rank} N + \dim \ker N = d$, so
$\operatorname{rank} N \le \dim \ker N = d - \operatorname{rank} N$, which
gives $2\operatorname{rank} N \le d$. For $d = 3$ that forces
$\operatorname{rank} N \le 1$, a single outer product $u\,v^{\mathsf T}$.

```{=html}
</details>
```

The simplest such pair is small and concrete:
$$
u = (1, -1, 0), \qquad v = (1, 1, -2),
$$
orthogonal, each summing to zero. Their outer product, scaled by
$\tfrac16$ so that $P + N$ stays non-negative, is
$$
N = \frac{1}{6}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & -2 \\ -1 & -1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix},
$$
and adding it to $P$ gives an honest copier,
$$
S = P + N = \begin{pmatrix} 1/2 & 1/2 & 0 \\ 1/6 & 1/6 & 2/3 \\ 1/3 & 1/3 & 1/3 \end{pmatrix},
$$
non-negative, with every row and column summing to one. By construction
$S^2 = P + N^2 = P$ while $S \ne P$, so this $S$ is a genuine square root
of total erasure: a copier that erases a three-state image in two equal
steps rather than one, funnelling every point along a two-step path to
the grey centre (@fig-root-d3). Up to relabelling the three states it is
the only such root, which is why the same matrix appears in the figure.

That same split hands us the general bound for free. For any $S = P + N$
in our class the cross terms always die, so $S^k = P + N^k$, and
$S^k = P$ exactly when $N^k = 0$. Erasing in exactly $k$ steps is nothing
more than $N$ being nilpotent of order $k$, and a nilpotent map on the
$(d-1)$-dimensional space of deviations from the grey centre runs out of
room after at most $d - 1$ steps. So the bound is
$$
k \le d - 1,
$$
already reached at $d = 3$ by the matrix above. (In the quantum upgrade
these deviations become the *traceless* operators, the same idea in
matrix language.)

```{=html}
<details class="aside">
<summary>Why the bound is reached in every dimension</summary>
```

A nilpotent $N$ is governed by its Jordan form, a stack of blocks each of
which powers to zero in exactly its own size. The largest block that fits
on the $(d-1)$-dimensional space of deviations is a single
$(d-1) \times (d-1)$ block with ones on the superdiagonal,
$$
N \;\cong\;
\begin{pmatrix}
0 & 1 & & & \\
 & 0 & 1 & & \\
 & & \ddots & \ddots & \\
 & & & 0 & 1 \\
 & & & & 0
\end{pmatrix}.
$$
Each power pushes that diagonal of ones one step toward the corner, so
$N^{d-1} = 0$ while $N^{d-2} \neq 0$. As long as $P + N$ can be kept
bistochastic, this very block gives a root of order exactly $d - 1$.

```{=html}
</details>
```

::: {#fig-root-d3}

{{< include figures/fig2-simplex-root/interactive.qmd >}}

One square root $S$ of the $d = 3$ bistochastic CDC (others exist),
animated on the simplex. A cloud of states, coloured by its
red-green-blue mixture, is sent to the centre in two equal steps: one application of
$S$ collapses the filled triangle onto a line segment, a second collapses
that segment onto the grey maximally mixed centre $p_0$, since $S^2 = P$,
and the colours drain toward grey as it goes. The three pure corners
trace highlighted paths; $e_1$ and $e_2$ land on the same intermediate
point $Se_1 = Se_2$, the merge that erases information in a stage. The
animation plays once when it scrolls into view; tap to replay.

:::

And that is the classical story. A clean bound, a clean construction,
and not much more to say about it.

The interesting thing is what happens to that bound when we let
ourselves leave classical probability behind.

<!-- =================================================================== -->
## The quantum upgrade {#sec-quantum}

Everything so far was a rehearsal. The real question is about quantum
information, and a quantum state carries more than a *classical*
probability distribution does. More in a way we can count, and the count
turns out to be the whole plot of this section.

Go back to the smallest example. A classical bit is one number: how a
coin is weighted between its two outcomes, $0$ and $1$. Picture that
number as a position on a line segment. The two ends are the only
*certain* states, "definitely $0$" and "definitely $1$"; every point
between is a blend, more or less uncertain, with the fair coin sitting at
the dead centre. One number, one dimension of freedom.

A quantum bit, a *qubit*, has more room, and the cleanest way to see how
much more is to ask what its *certain* states are. (Quantum mechanics
also allows genuine superpositions, the $\alpha\,|0\rangle + \beta\,|1\rangle$
of the amplitude picture,[^qcvc] but for a story about forgetting we want
the geometry of states, not the algebra of amplitudes.) Classically there
were exactly two certain states, the two ends of the line. A qubit has
infinitely many. That is one of the genuine surprises of quantum
mechanics, and not one this post can derive; we take it as given and
simply draw it. The certain states no longer sit at two points. They
fill the entire surface of a ball.

This is not a mathematical fiction. Two everyday incarnations make it
concrete. The polarization of a photon is a qubit: a filter aligned with
it passes the photon every time, a filter at right angles blocks it, and
one at $45^\circ$ lets it through half the time. So is the spin of an
electron: point a detector along the spin and you always read the same
way, turn the detector sideways and the outcome goes random. In each, the
certain states are not two but a whole continuum, one for every angle you
could set the filter or the detector to.

That continuum is the surface of the qubit's state space, the *Bloch
ball* (@fig-bloch). Picture a state as an arrow inside the ball, with a
direction and a length. The *length* says how certain the state is:
arrows reaching the surface are the certain, *pure* states, shorter
arrows are blurrier mixtures, and the zero-length arrow at the dead
centre is total ignorance, the quantum coin flip. The *direction* says
which question the state answers with certainty. Every direction names a
measurement you could make, and the state pointing that way is the one
whose outcome you can predict. The poles are the ordinary question, "are
you $0$ or $1$?", and the classical bit's two states sit there. A state
out on the equator answers that question with a perfect coin flip, yet is
itself perfectly definite, just for a *different* question. Ask a qubit
the wrong question and the answer turns random; that, and not fuzziness,
is what the surface is encoding.

The object that bookkeeps this arrow is a small matrix, the *density
matrix*, but you need only its shape here, not its inner workings.

[^qcvc]: We meet qubits, density matrices, and channels here at the
level of pictures, not bra-ket algebra, so you can follow along cold. If
you want the real foundations, single qubits, gates, and the
$|0\rangle, |1\rangle$ notation built from scratch, Matuschak and
Nielsen's [Quantum Computing for the Very Curious](https://quantum.country/qcvc)
is the gentlest on-ramp I know, and it is the model this post is written
in.

::: {#fig-bloch}

{{< include figures/fig3-bloch-ball/interactive.qmd >}}

The Bloch ball, the state space of a single qubit: pure states live on the surface, mixed states inside, and the maximally mixed state $I/2$ sits at the centre. Compare the classical bit, whose states fill only a line segment. This is the quantum counterpart of the simplex in @fig-simplex-d3. Click the front of the ball to pick a direction, and use the Purity slider to slide the state inward from the surface; the readout names the one measurement that direction answers with certainty, and how that certainty fades as the state mixes.

:::

Notice what happened to the dimension. The classical bit lived on a
line, one dimension; the qubit fills a ball, *three*. That jump is the
pattern worth chasing, but to count it for any number of levels we first
have to say what a quantum state even is beyond the qubit.

We met the qubit's state as an arrow, bookkept by a small matrix. For
$d$ levels the bookkeeping object is the same kind of thing, a
$d \times d$ matrix called the *density matrix*, and its rules are not
arbitrary: they are exactly what it takes to still be describing
probabilities. The matrix is Hermitian, so its eigenvalues are real;
those eigenvalues are non-negative and sum to one. That last clause is
the point, because non-negative numbers summing to one are a probability
distribution. A density matrix is a classical probability distribution in
disguise: its eigenvalues are the probabilities, and its eigenvectors say
which mutually exclusive pure states they are spread across. The
classical simplex from the first half of this post is the special case
where the axes have already been chosen for you.

Now we can count. A quantum state in dimension $d$ is pinned down by
$d^2 - 1$ real numbers.

```{=html}
<details class="aside">
<summary>Where $d^2 - 1$ comes from</summary>
```

A $d \times d$ Hermitian matrix is fixed by $d^2$ real numbers: $d$
real numbers on the diagonal, plus the entries above the diagonal,
each complex and so worth two reals, with everything below the diagonal
forced by Hermiticity. The off-diagonal count is $2 \cdot \tfrac{d(d-1)}{2} = d(d-1)$,
and $d + d(d-1) = d^2$. Fixing the trace to one removes a single degree
of freedom, leaving $d^2 - 1$.

```{=html}
</details>
```

So the quantum state space is $(d^2 - 1)$-dimensional, against the
classical simplex's $d - 1$. For a single bit, three against one. The
freedom grew *quadratically*, and every result in this post is a shadow
of that one fact.

The rest of the cast carries over almost unchanged. A quantum copier is
a *channel*: a linear map that turns density matrices into density
matrices. It has to be linear for exactly the reason it was classically,
that a coin-flip mixture of inputs must come out as the same coin-flip
mixture of outputs. There is one extra demand with no classical echo,
called *complete positivity*, which insists the map keeps sending valid
states to valid states even when it acts on only part of a larger
entangled system. Channels are well understood objects with a clean
structure theory.[^channels] For us they are simply the right notion of
"physically allowed operation," and we will not pry them open.

[^channels]: For the structure theory of quantum channels, including
the Kraus decomposition and the Stinespring dilation, the standard
reference is Nielsen and Chuang, *Quantum Computation and Quantum
Information*, chapter 8. Michael Wolf's lecture notes *Quantum Channels
and Operations: Guided Tour* are a more focused modern treatment.

We make the same restriction we made classically. Out of all channels
we keep the ones that leave the state of total ignorance untouched.
Classically that was the uniform distribution. Here it is the *maximally
mixed state*, the centre of the Bloch ball, written $I/d$ with $I$ the
identity matrix. A channel that fixes it invents no information from
nothing and secretly prefers no state to any other, which is the least
we should ask of a process whose only job is to forget. (Such channels
have a name, *unital*, but the name matters less than the picture.)

Total erasure is the same idea as before, too. The *completely
depolarising channel* sends every input, no exceptions, to the maximally
mixed state. The whole Bloch ball collapses to its centre point in a
single step. This is the quantum CDC, and it is the operator we now want
to take roots of.

Here is where that quadratic shows up where it counts. Ask the same
question as in the classical case: how large can $k$ be, if a channel
$S$ satisfies $S^k = P$ but no smaller power does? The argument has the
same skeleton. The quantum CDC is again a rank-one map: it sends the
entire space of traceless operators, the directions away from the
maximally mixed state, to zero. Any $S$ powering to it must carry a
*nilpotent* part on that space, and a single nilpotent block on a space
of dimension $D$ takes at most $D$ steps to wind down. Only now
$D = d^2 - 1$ rather than $d - 1$, so
$$
k \;\leq\; d^2 - 1.
$$

Set $d = 2$. The classical bound was $k \leq 1$: a single bit could not
be erased in more than one step. The quantum bound is $k \leq 3$. Three
gentle steps to forget one qubit (@fig-bloch-root), where one classical
bit allowed only the abrupt single step. The room to subdivide erasure
grew, and it grew quadratically.

::: {#fig-bloch-root}

{{< include figures/fig3b-bloch-root/interactive.qmd >}}

A maximal qubit root $S$ acting on the Bloch ball (others exist). It
sends a Bloch vector $(r_1, r_2, r_3)$ to $(r_2/2,\, r_3/2,\, 0)$,
driving every state
to the centre $I/2$ in at most three steps, and the $z$-pole takes all
three, realising the order-3 bound ($d^2 - 1 = 3$ at $d = 2$). As with
the classical square root in @fig-root-d3, erasure happens in stages:
each step both shrinks the vector and rotates it onto the next axis.
Directions already in the channel's kernel (here the $x$-axis) collapse
sooner; the slowest direction sets the order. The animation drives a
whole cloud of Bloch vectors to $I/2$ through these stages and picks out
the three axis orbits (the blue $z$-pole is the hero that takes all
three steps); it plays once when it scrolls into view, and you can tap to
replay.

:::

One honest caveat before we move on, and it is really the seed of the
rest of the post. That $d^2 - 1$ is only an *upper* bound. It comes from
a structural argument: on the $d^2 - 1$ traceless directions, place the
longest nilpotent Jordan block that fits, and its powers take exactly
$d^2 - 1$ steps to vanish. That conjures a *linear map* of the right
order, but a linear map is not yet a quantum channel. The binding
constraint is complete positivity, and when I first sat with this problem
it was not at all clear to me that a map assembled by wedging in a Jordan
block stays completely positive. The bound might be a mirage, an order no
genuine channel can reach.

That doubt is what sent me to Clifford channels. Rather than try to
settle by hand whether a Jordan-block construction stays completely
positive, I turned to a much smaller, more structured family of channels:
far less freedom, but every member a genuine channel by construction, and
a class that has proved fruitful before across quantum information. The
question then becomes concrete and answerable by direct computation, how
large can the order grow inside this restricted family. (It does turn out
that the full bound is reachable, by a construction subtler than a raw
Jordan block; that is a thread for the end of the post.)

<!-- =================================================================== -->
## Coordinates for the Paulis {#sec-paulis}

We left the last section with a promise and a worry. The promise: rather
than search the whole space of channels for one that reaches the
$d^2 - 1$ bound, we would work inside a small, structured family where
every member is a genuine channel by construction. The worry was what
sent us there, that it was not clear, certainly not to me at the time,
whether the bound-saturating Jordan block is a legal channel at all.
Before we can pin that family down, we need a good way to handle the
operators it is built from. This short interlude builds exactly that: a
clean little arithmetic we lean on for the rest of the post.

Start with what we have already been drawing. The three axes of the Bloch
ball are not anonymous directions; each is a matrix, the *Pauli matrices*
$$
X = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad
Y = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -i \\ i & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad
Z = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix},
$$
with the identity $I$ at the centre. The $x$, $y$, $z$ axes of the ball
are $X$, $Y$, $Z$. Everything a qubit can do is built from these four
matrices.

They make convenient handles because they multiply into one another.
Square any one and you return to the identity, $X^2 = Y^2 = Z^2 = I$.
Multiply two different ones and you get the third, with a phase out
front,
$$
XY = iZ, \qquad YZ = iX, \qquad ZX = iY,
$$
and the order is not free: reverse it and the phase flips sign,
$XZ = -iY$ against $ZX = iY$. The cleanest way to hold all of this at once
is a small multiplication table, read as row times column:

| $\cdot$ | $I$ | $X$ | $Y$ | $Z$ |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| $I$ | $I$ | $X$ | $Y$ | $Z$ |
| $X$ | $X$ | $I$ | $iZ$ | $-iY$ |
| $Y$ | $Y$ | $-iZ$ | $I$ | $iX$ |
| $Z$ | $Z$ | $iY$ | $-iX$ | $I$ |

Try to keep only $\{I, X, Y, Z\}$ and you cannot: the stray factors of
$i$ and $-1$ refuse to leave. Let them in and you get a small, closed,
finite collection,
$$
\{\, \pm I, \pm iI,\ \pm X, \pm iX,\ \pm Y, \pm iY,\ \pm Z, \pm iZ \,\},
$$
sixteen matrices that multiply among themselves and nowhere else. That
collection is the *Pauli group*, the entire vocabulary of one qubit.

Sixteen elements with sign-and-$i$ bookkeeping sounds fiddly, but nearly
all of the fiddliness is the phases, and we can quarantine them. Track
only *which* Pauli you are holding, ignoring any $\pm 1$ or $\pm i$ in
front, and the multiplication collapses to something you could do in your
head. Tag each Pauli with two bits, the first asking "does it flip?", the
second "does it add a phase?":
$$
I = (0,0), \qquad X = (1,0), \qquad Z = (0,1), \qquad Y = (1,1).
$$
Now multiplying Paulis is just *adding* the tags, entry by entry, modulo
two. $X$ times $Z$ ought to flip and phase at once: $(1,0) + (0,1) =
(1,1)$, which is $Y$. Exactly right. The four Paulis have become the four
points of a tiny grid, and their multiplication has become addition.

One thing refused to come along: the phase. In shrugging off "any
$\pm i$ in front" we discarded real information, the very $-1$ behind
$XZ = -ZX$ in the table. Adding tags remembers *which* Pauli you land on
but forgets the phase you collect getting there. Holding both at once,
the tidy tag-addition and a phase trailing behind it, is what makes this
a *projective* picture rather than a plain one. We need no machinery for
the word, only the attitude: the labels are a clean plane to navigate,
and a phase quietly rides along on top. Keep both in view, because that
trailing phase is not noise to be thrown away. It is the seam the next
section pries open.

None of this leaned on there being two levels. Give the system $d$ levels
instead of two and the same story unfolds with more dots. The Paulis grow
into $d^2$ operators, the *Weyl operators* $\mathbf{w}(\eta)$, each tagged
by a pair $\eta = (a, b)$ whose entries now run $0, 1, \ldots, d - 1$
rather than just $0$ and $1$. They still form a basis of every
$d \times d$ matrix, so a channel is fixed by what it does to them; they
still multiply by adding tags, now modulo $d$; and they still do so only
up to a trailing phase, now a $d$-th root of unity $\omega = e^{2\pi i/d}$
in place of a sign. The tags no longer fill a $2 \times 2$ square but a
$d \times d$ grid, the plane we will write $\mathbb{F}_d^2$.

One label stands apart on that grid. The origin $(0,0)$ is the identity,
the trace direction every channel in our class must leave untouched. That
leaves $d^2 - 1$ nonzero labels, the directions that can genuinely be
forgotten, and they are exactly the $d^2 - 1$ dimensions we counted on the
Bloch ball, come back as the nonzero points of a finite grid. (One feature
of the grid will matter later: it behaves like a full number system, where
you can divide as freely as you add and multiply, only when $d$ is prime.
We will not need division until the labels start moving, and the explicit
shift-and-phase recipe for $\mathbf{w}(\eta)$ is one fold away.)

```{=html}
<details class="aside">
<summary>The Weyl operators explicitly, and why $d$ must be prime</summary>
```

Fix $d$ levels, $|0\rangle$ through $|d-1\rangle$. Two elementary moves
generate everything. The first is a *shift* that bumps every level up by
one and wraps around at the top, $X\colon|j\rangle \mapsto |j+1\rangle$,
the higher-dimensional bit-flip. The second is a *phase kick* that
multiplies level $j$ by a $d$-th root of unity,
$Z\colon|j\rangle \mapsto \omega^{\,j}|j\rangle$ with
$\omega = e^{2\pi i/d}$, the higher-dimensional phase-flip. Applying $a$
shifts and $b$ phase kicks gives the Weyl operator
$\mathbf{w}(a,b) \sim X^a Z^b$, fixed up to a phase convention we never
need; there are $d^2$ of them, one for each label $(a,b)$ with $a$ and
$b$ taken modulo $d$. At $d = 2$ they are just the four Paulis renamed.

Multiply two and the labels add, up to that same phase:
$\mathbf{w}(\eta)\,\mathbf{w}(\xi) = (\text{phase}) \cdot \mathbf{w}(\eta + \xi)$.
The labels add exactly, but the operators reproduce that addition only up
to a phase, which is why the assignment is called a *projective*
representation of the group of labels; we never need the phase's exact
form. As for the primality: the integers modulo a prime form a *field*
$\mathbb{F}_d$, in which division works as cleanly as addition,
subtraction and multiplication. We will need to divide by labels, not
merely add them, once the labels start moving around the plane, and
division behaves only when $d$ is prime.

```{=html}
</details>
```

That is the whole stage: a plane of labels $\mathbb{F}_d^2$, with a phase
trailing along whenever you multiply. Everything left in this post plays
out on it. The channels we are about to single out do just two things to
this plane. They *relabel* it, sending each point to another by a single
linear map, each axis to an axis. And at each label they pin on a number
of their own, a phase that is also allowed to shrink in size. That
attached number is where forgetting will live, and following it around
the plane is how we hunt down the long roots. Time to meet the channels.

<!-- =================================================================== -->
## Clifford channels as the playground {#sec-clifford}

Recall what we are after. The completely depolarising channel $P$ erases
every input in a single step, and we want to write it as $P = S^k$ for a
channel $S$ that takes as many identical steps as possible to accomplish
the same erasure, to subdivide total forgetting as finely as we can. We
already know the prize is bounded: any such $S$ must act nilpotently on
the $d^2 - 1$ traceless directions, so $k \le d^2 - 1$. But that bound
came from a counting argument that constructs nothing, and to learn
whether it can actually be reached we would like to exhibit a channel
that reaches it. The obvious move is to go searching in the full space of
channels, and here we run into trouble. That space is forbiddingly large;
its dimension grows like $d^4$. Worse, the condition that singles out the
physically allowed maps, complete positivity, is not a list of
independent bounds on the parameters but a single global positivity
requirement on the Choi matrix. As one varies the entries, tracking where
that requirement holds is already delicate for a qutrit and quickly
becomes hopeless to oversee in higher dimensions. We would rather not
confront this space head-on.

To decide what restriction to impose, it helps to look first at the one
case we can actually draw, the single qubit. Its states fill the Bloch
ball, and a unital channel (one that fixes the maximally mixed state at
the centre) is pinned down entirely by what it does to the three
coordinate axes; once we know where the axes go, linearity supplies
everything in between. And those axes are the Paulis $X$, $Y$, $Z$ we
met in the interlude, with the identity at the centre. A general channel
is free to send each of them wherever it
pleases. The image of the $X$ axis may tilt off into some blend of all
three directions, the ball is squashed into a skewed, shrunken ellipsoid,
and the three clean axes we began with end up smeared into one another.
This is precisely the freedom we just called hard to oversee: there is
simply too much room in where the axes may land.

Let us impose a rather strong restriction on the map. Rather than letting
the axes wander, we demand that each Pauli be carried to a single Pauli,
at most rescaled: the $X$ axis goes to a multiple of one coordinate axis,
never to a mixture of them. Geometrically the ellipsoid is no longer
allowed to tumble: its principal axes stay aligned with the originals,
permuted among themselves and stretched or squeezed, but never rotated
into off-axis directions. The rule already has a pedigree. The unitaries
that send Paulis to Paulis under conjugation are exactly the *Clifford
group*, the well-behaved gates at the heart of quantum error correction.
The maps we have just described are their dissipative relatives: they
keep the same Paulis-to-Paulis bookkeeping, but they are allowed to
*shrink* an axis rather than merely permute it, and it is in that
shrinking that forgetting will live. We call them *Clifford channels*.

::: {#fig-clifford-grid}

{{< include figures/fig5-continuum-grid/interactive.qmd >}}

Left: the qubit state space, a continuum that a general channel can
deform into an ellipsoid at any angle. Right: the four labels $(a, b)$,
with $a$ counting bit-flips and $b$ phase-flips, so $(1,0)$, $(0,1)$,
$(1,1)$ are the $X$, $Z$, $Y$ axes and $(0,0)$ is the identity. A
Clifford channel may stretch or swap the three coloured axes but never
tilt them, so all of its "where each direction goes" freedom is the map
$h$ permuting these finitely many points. The origin $(0,0)$, the
identity every copier fixes, stays put; for the qubit, $h$ is just a
permutation of the other three.

:::

In the interlude we gave every Pauli an address on the plane
$\mathbb{F}_d^2$ and saw that multiplying Paulis just adds their
addresses. A Clifford channel's relabelling has to respect that addition,
which pins it down: it must be a *linear* map of the plane, an invertible
$2 \times 2$ matrix $h$ over $\mathbb{F}_d$ (two distinct axes can never be
folded onto one place). For the qubit there are only $3! = 6$ of them, the
permutations of the three nonzero labels; the one drawn in the figure is
the three-cycle
$$
h = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \qquad \text{over } \mathbb{F}_2,
$$
cycling $(1,0) \to (0,1) \to (1,1) \to (1,0)$ and fixing the origin.

We can now say precisely which channels we keep. Apply a general channel
to a single Weyl operator and you get back a sprawling combination of all
$d^2$ of them. A *Clifford channel* refuses the sprawl: it sends each
Weyl operator to a single other Weyl operator, rescaled,
$$
T[\mathbf{w}(\eta)] = \lambda(\eta)\,\mathbf{w}(h(\eta)).
$$
It carries exactly two pieces of data. The first is the relabelling $h$
we just met, the invertible linear map of the label plane that shuffles
the axes among themselves. The second is $\lambda$, the list of
amplitudes: one number $\lambda(\eta)$ for each label, the factor by which
that coordinate is stretched or shrunk. This is where forgetting lives. An
amplitude below one in magnitude damps a coordinate, and an amplitude
equal to zero erases it outright. Take $h$ the three-cycle above with
every $\lambda(\eta) = 1$, and the channel merely shuffles the axes and
forgets nothing, a reversible relabelling; forgetting begins only when
some amplitude drops below one, which is what the coming sections are about.

It is worth pausing on how little data this is. A general channel in
dimension $d$ is described by its Choi matrix, an object of size
$d^2 \times d^2$ carrying on the order of $d^4$ free numbers, all of them
laced together by the global positivity condition we balked at earlier. A
Clifford channel is a single $2 \times 2$ matrix over the finite field
$\mathbb{F}_d$ together with a list of $d^2$ amplitudes. The two pieces
are not even the same kind of object: the relabelling $h$ is one choice
out of a finite set, while the amplitudes $\lambda$ are the only
continuous freedom that remains. We have kept a tiny corner of the space
of channels.

With the class fixed, we return to the question we actually care about:
we want a Clifford channel $S$ that is a root of total erasure,
$S^k = P$, with $k$ as large as we can make it. Before going further it
is worth asking whether this is even a sensible place to look, and two
facts reassure us. First, the target itself belongs to the class. The
completely depolarising channel fixes the identity and annihilates every
other Weyl operator, precisely the Clifford form with the trivial
relabelling and every amplitude but the central one set to zero. We are
not chasing something that lives outside our playground. Second, the
class is closed under composition: feed one Clifford channel into another
and the relabellings compose while the amplitudes multiply, so every
power $S^k$ is again a Clifford channel. The whole equation $S^k = P$
thus plays out inside the class; taking roots never forces us back into
the wilderness of general channels.

What is *not* guaranteed is that this corner is large enough. It is
entirely possible that, in giving up so much freedom, we have driven the
achievable $k$ back down toward the classical $d - 1$, making the
restriction a poor bargain. Whether the room to subdivide erasure
survives this drastic narrowing is exactly what the next sections settle,
and the reason we can settle it, rather than merely hope, is that powers
of a Clifford channel are transparent in a way powers of a general
channel never are. To that transparency we now turn.

<!-- =================================================================== -->
## The reduction (the pivot) {#sec-reduction}

We left off promising to iterate. So let us iterate, and watch.

Apply $T$ to a single Weyl operator. By definition it comes back
rescaled and relabelled:
$$
T[\mathbf{w}(\eta)] = \lambda(\eta)\,\mathbf{w}(h(\eta)).
$$
Now apply $T$ again. The output is itself a Weyl operator, so $T$ knows
exactly what to do with it:
$$
T^2[\mathbf{w}(\eta)] = \lambda(\eta)\,T[\mathbf{w}(h(\eta))]
= \lambda(\eta)\,\lambda(h(\eta))\,\mathbf{w}(h^2(\eta)).
$$
Apply it $n$ times and the pattern is plain:
$$
T^n[\mathbf{w}(\eta)] = \Biggl(\prod_{j=0}^{n-1} \lambda\bigl(h^j(\eta)\bigr)\Biggr)\,\mathbf{w}\bigl(h^n(\eta)\bigr).
$$

Sit with that for a moment, because the fog has lifted completely.

Iterating the channel did two clean, separate things. The label moved,
$\eta \to h(\eta) \to h^2(\eta) \to \cdots$, a single point hopping
around the plane $\mathbb{F}_d^2$ under repeated application of the one
matrix $h$. And an amplitude piled up, a running product of $\lambda$
values, one factor collected at each label the point lands on.

That sequence of labels, $\eta, h(\eta), h^2(\eta), \ldots$, is the
*orbit* of $\eta$ under $h$. The entire life of the channel, run any
number of times, is bookkept by two finite-field facts: how the orbit
travels, and what $\lambda$ does along it. The infinite-dimensional
machinery of quantum channels has collapsed into a point hopping around
a plane of $d^2$ labels, multiplying numbers as it goes.

Now recall what we are chasing. The completely depolarising channel $P$
erases everything: it leaves the identity $\mathbf{w}(0)$ alone and
annihilates every other Weyl operator,
$$
P[\mathbf{w}(\eta)] = 0 \quad \text{for every } \eta \neq 0.
$$
That is just "every state goes to the maximally mixed state," written in
the Weyl coordinate system. The identity label takes care of itself:
$\lambda(0) = 1$ because the channel preserves the trace, so
$\mathbf{w}(0)$ is fixed at every step. All the action is on the
$d^2 - 1$ nonzero labels.

So asking for $T^k = P$ is asking for the accumulated amplitude to be
*zero* on every nonzero label after exactly $k$ steps:
$$
\prod_{j=0}^{k-1} \lambda\bigl(h^j(\eta)\bigr) = 0
\qquad \text{for every } \eta \neq 0.
$$
A product of numbers is zero exactly when one of its factors is. So the
condition says something you can picture: travelling along the orbit of
any nonzero $\eta$, within the first $k$ steps the point must pass
through at least one label where $\lambda$ vanishes. And $k$ has to be
the *smallest* such number, since we want the erasure to land at step
$k$ and not a step sooner. Push $k$ as high as it will go while still
erasing every orbit, and you have found the longest root.

This is the pivot of the whole post, so let me state it with no quantum
mechanics in the sentence at all. We want a point that, started anywhere
nonzero and moved repeatedly by $h$, takes as long as possible to first
land on a label where $\lambda$ vanishes. Two things govern that delay,
and they are independent:

1. **How long the orbits are.** If $h$ carries a point through many
   distinct labels before it repeats, there is more room to postpone the
   first vanishing. This is a question about the matrix $h$ by itself:
   its *order*, and how it cuts the $d^2 - 1$ nonzero labels into orbits.
   That is the next section.

2. **Where $\lambda$ is allowed to vanish.** We need $\lambda$ to hit
   zero at least once on every orbit, but as late as possible. And
   $\lambda$ is not free to vanish wherever it pleases: a constraint
   inherited from complete positivity forces its zeros to come in pairs,
   and that pairing is exactly what costs us a factor of two. That is the
   section after.

Solve those two and the bound drops out. The astonishing part, already
half in view, is that neither question mentions a quantum channel any
more. From here on we are doing linear algebra over a finite field.

<!-- =================================================================== -->
## Ingredient 1: the order of $h$ {#sec-ingredient-h}

The first ingredient is the easy one to state. We want the point to
visit as many labels as possible before it starts repeating, so we want
the orbits of $h$ to be long. How long can they get?

There are $d^2 - 1$ nonzero labels in all, so no orbit can be longer
than that. The happy fact is that the maximum is reached. There exist
matrices $h$ in $GL(2, \mathbb{F}_d)$ whose single orbit sweeps through
*every* nonzero label before returning home: one grand cycle of length
$d^2 - 1$, visiting all of $\mathbb{F}_d^2 \setminus \{0\}$. Such an $h$
acts *transitively* on the nonzero labels.

Where do these maximal matrices come from? From a second field hiding
inside the first. The plane $\mathbb{F}_d^2$ is two-dimensional over
$\mathbb{F}_d$, and it happens to also *be* a larger field, the field
$\mathbb{F}_{d^2}$ with $d^2$ elements. In any finite field the nonzero
elements, multiplied together, form a single cycle: there is a
*generator* whose powers run through every nonzero element exactly once.
Multiplication by that generator is an $\mathbb{F}_d$-linear map on the
plane, and as a matrix it is our maximal $h$.

```{=html}
<details class="aside">
<summary>Primitive polynomials, and why the order is exactly $d^2 - 1$</summary>
```

A *primitive polynomial* of degree two over $\mathbb{F}_d$ is an
irreducible quadratic whose root generates the multiplicative group of
$\mathbb{F}_{d^2}$. Call that root $g$. Its powers
$g, g^2, g^3, \ldots$ cycle through all $d^2 - 1$ nonzero elements of
$\mathbb{F}_{d^2}$ before $g^{\,d^2 - 1} = 1$ brings them back, so $g$
has multiplicative order exactly $d^2 - 1$.

Viewing $\mathbb{F}_{d^2}$ as the plane $\mathbb{F}_d^2$, multiplication
by $g$ is a linear map, and in a basis it is the *companion matrix* of
the primitive polynomial. It inherits the order $d^2 - 1$, and that is
the largest order any element of $GL(2, \mathbb{F}_d)$ can have. (Every
other kind of element, the diagonalisable ones and the single-eigenvalue
ones, tops out lower; the irreducible "Singer" elements like this one are
the champions.)

```{=html}
</details>
```

It pays to see one. Take $d = 3$, so we are working modulo $3$ and the
plane has $3^2 - 1 = 8$ nonzero points. The polynomial $x^2 + x + 2$ is
primitive over $\mathbb{F}_3$, and its companion matrix is
$$
h = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}.
$$
Start at the label $(1,0)$ and apply $h$ over and over, doing all the
arithmetic modulo $3$:
$$
(1,0) \to (0,1) \to (1,2) \to (2,2) \to (2,0) \to (0,2) \to (2,1) \to (1,1) \to (1,0).
$$
Eight steps, eight distinct labels, every nonzero point of the plane
visited exactly once, and then home. This $h$ has order $8 = 3^2 - 1$,
the most a $2 \times 2$ matrix over $\mathbb{F}_3$ can manage. One orbit,
as long as the plane allows.

If $\lambda$ could vanish at just a single point of this cycle, we would
be done, and we would reach the full quantum bound: a point starting one
step past the lone zero would have to travel all $d^2 - 1$ steps to come
back to it. That would be a root of order $d^2 - 1$. But $\lambda$ cannot
vanish at only one point, and the reason is the second ingredient.

<!-- =================================================================== -->
## Ingredient 2: orbits and where $\lambda$ vanishes {#sec-ingredient-lambda}

So we need $\lambda$ to vanish somewhere on the orbit, and we would like
it to vanish as rarely as possible, ideally just once. Here the channel
pushes back. The amplitudes $\lambda$ are not ours to set freely, and the
constraint comes in two layers.

The first layer is a symmetry. A quantum channel $T$ sends Hermitian
operators to Hermitian operators, since the density matrices it acts on
are Hermitian. Tracing what that requires of the amplitudes gives a clean
relation between the label $\eta$ and its negative:
$$
\lambda(-\eta) = \overline{\lambda(\eta)}.
$$
Take absolute values and the consequence is stark:
$|\lambda(-\eta)| = |\lambda(\eta)|$. The amplitude at a label and the
amplitude at its mirror image always have the same size. In particular,
**if $\lambda$ vanishes at $\eta$, it must vanish at $-\eta$ as well.**
The zeros come in mirror pairs.

The second layer is stronger, and we will lean on it shortly. A channel
is not merely required to preserve Hermiticity; it must be *completely
positive*. That places a further positivity condition on a matrix built
from the values of $\lambda$, one the mirror-pair symmetry alone does not
guarantee. We will come back to it once we have seen what the mirror
pairing already forces.

```{=html}
<details class="aside">
<summary>The Hermiticity argument</summary>
```

This relation comes from $T$ preserving Hermiticity, a property shared by
every quantum channel but in itself weaker than full complete positivity.
A Weyl operator is not Hermitian, but its adjoint is another Weyl
operator: $\mathbf{w}(\eta)^\dagger = \mathbf{w}(-\eta)$, up to the same
phase convention we have been ignoring. A channel obeys
$T[A^\dagger] = T[A]^\dagger$, because it must turn Hermitian inputs into
Hermitian outputs. Apply this to $A = \mathbf{w}(\eta)$. On one side,
$T[\mathbf{w}(\eta)^\dagger] = T[\mathbf{w}(-\eta)] = \lambda(-\eta)\,\mathbf{w}(h(-\eta))$.
On the other, $T[\mathbf{w}(\eta)]^\dagger = \overline{\lambda(\eta)}\,\mathbf{w}(h(\eta))^\dagger = \overline{\lambda(\eta)}\,\mathbf{w}(-h(\eta))$.
Since $h$ is linear, $h(-\eta) = -h(\eta)$, so the two Weyl operators
match and the coefficients must agree: $\lambda(-\eta) = \overline{\lambda(\eta)}$.

```{=html}
</details>
```

Now put the two ingredients together, and here is something worth
pausing on. The mirror-pair constraint pairs every nonzero label $\eta$
with its negative $-\eta$, and for odd prime $d$ those are always
distinct points of the plane. The grand cycle has length $d^2 - 1$, an
even number, and the mirror map $\eta \mapsto -\eta$ sends you exactly
halfway around it. The two paired zeros sit at opposite poles of the
cycle, cutting it into two equal arcs of length $(d^2 - 1)/2$;
@fig-orbit shows the $d = 3$ case.

What about $d = 2$? At $d = 2$ arithmetic is modulo $2$, so $-1 = 1$, and
every label is its own mirror. The pairing constraint collapses: it no
longer forces a second zero anywhere. A single vanishing of $\lambda$ on
the three-element cycle is enough, and the longest possible delay is the
full cycle length, $3$. That is exactly the general quantum bound
$d^2 - 1 = 3$.

So the qubit is not an awkward edge case. It is the one case where
Clifford channels already saturate the full quantum bound, because the
symmetry tax that costs a factor of $2$ for larger $d$ does not apply at
$d = 2$. The factor-of-two gap between Clifford and general opens up at
$d = 3$ and stays open from then on.

![The grand orbit of $h$ for $d = 3$: the eight nonzero
labels arranged in the cycle
$(1,0) \to (0,1) \to \cdots \to (1,1) \to (1,0)$. The mirror symmetry
forces the zeros of $\lambda$ into a pair (here $(1,0)$ and its
antipode $(2,0)$), splitting the cycle into two arcs of four steps
each.](figures/orbit-d3.svg){#fig-orbit}

And that settles it. Whichever point you start from, you reach one of
the two zeros within half a turn of the cycle. The longest you can be
made to wait is the length of one arc, $(d^2 - 1)/2$ steps.

One technical point remains, and I would rather flag it than slip past.
Choosing where $\lambda$ vanishes is not the same as proving that such a
$\lambda$ comes from a genuinely completely positive channel. This is the
second layer from a moment ago: complete positivity asks a certain matrix
assembled from the values of $\lambda$ to be positive semidefinite, and
the mirror pairing alone does not deliver it. It can be met, though. Keep
the nonzero amplitudes modest away from the paired zeros and the channel
stays completely positive, so suitable $\lambda$ do exist; we simply do
not get free run of the whole half-cycle. The thesis works the positivity
criterion out in full (§5.2.1).

With that secured, we have built a Clifford channel that erases in exactly
$$
k = \frac{d^2 - 1}{2}
$$
steps and no fewer. A Clifford root of the completely depolarising
channel of that order exists.

For our qutrit, $d = 3$, that is a root of order $4$: four gentle steps
to erase a qutrit using nothing but the two-piece Clifford data. The
mirror pair of zeros sits at $(1,0)$ and $(2,0)$ in the cycle above, and
every other label is at most four steps from one of them.

<!-- =================================================================== -->
## Punchline {#sec-punchline}

Line up the three bounds. How finely can you divide total erasure, the
completely depolarising channel, into equal steps?

- Classically, with a bistochastic copier: $d - 1$ steps.
- With a general quantum channel: $d^2 - 1$ steps.
- With a Clifford channel: $d^2 - 1$ at $d = 2$, dropping to
  $\dfrac{d^2 - 1}{2}$ for $d$ an odd prime.

For a qubit ($d = 2$): $1$ classically, $3$ generally, $3$ with Clifford
channels. The qubit is the case where the Clifford toolbox is already the
full toolbox.

For a qutrit ($d = 3$): $2$ classically, $8$ generally, $4$ with Clifford
channels. Here the gap opens. The Clifford copier, carrying almost no
information about itself, lands at $4$: within a factor of two of the
full quantum power of $8$, and already twice the classical $2$.

That is the part worth carrying away. When we restricted from all
quantum channels down to Clifford channels, we threw away almost all the
freedom. A general channel needs of order $d^4$ numbers to describe; a
Clifford channel needs a $2 \times 2$ matrix over $\mathbb{F}_d$ and a
short list of amplitudes. You might have guessed the bound would
collapse most of the way back to the classical $d - 1$. It barely moved.

The reason is that the room to subdivide erasure never lived in the
richness of the channel in the first place. It lived in the orbit
structure of a single linear map on a small finite plane. The longest
root is as long as the longest orbit of $h$, and a well-chosen $h$ runs
through all $d^2 - 1$ labels at once. The only thing the quantum
machinery buys you over this finite-field skeleton is the factor of two,
and even that is not channel richness: it is the one symmetry,
$\lambda(-\eta) = \overline{\lambda(\eta)}$, that Hermiticity preservation
stamps on the amplitudes and nothing more.

A question that began with photocopiers and density matrices turns out
to be answered, almost entirely, by asking how long a point can wander
in the plane $\mathbb{F}_d^2$ before it is forced to step on a marked
square. That is the unreasonable beauty promised at the top.

<!-- =================================================================== -->
## What's next {#sec-closing}

One loose thread remains: the factor of two. Is $(d^2 - 1)/2$ the end of
the story, or just the end of the *Clifford* story? It is only the
Clifford story. The full quantum bound $d^2 - 1$ really can be reached,
by a channel that gives up the tidy Weyl structure we leaned on. Instead
of asking a single matrix $h$ to do all the work, one builds the root
directly at the level of the channel's representation, nudging a Jordan
block into exactly the shape the bound allows. That construction does
not care about mirror pairs, so the factor of two disappears, and the
gap to $d^2 - 1$ closes.

That more general result subsumes the Clifford one, which is why the
Clifford construction does not appear in the final paper. I wanted to
write it up anyway, because it is the cleanest place I know to actually
*see* the finite-field representation theory at work. In the general
construction the orbit structure is buried inside linear algebra over
$\mathbb{C}$. Here it sits on the surface: a point hopping around a plane
of $d^2$ labels, a matrix of order $d^2 - 1$, and a single symmetry that
costs a factor of two. The whole argument fits in the palm of your hand,
and you can check the $d = 3$ case by stepping around an eight-point
cycle with a pencil.

The full development, including the classical and general quantum bounds
and the Clifford channels above, is in my diploma thesis.
